flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Scarlet Carnation
flowers.description: Ohio's state flower is the scarlet carnation — chosen in honor of President William McKinley, an Ohioan who wore one as a good luck charm. Not a native wildflower but deeply embedded in Ohio's cultural identity.

flowers.name: Trillium (White)
flowers.description: Ohio's most celebrated native wildflower — large pure white three-petaled flowers aging to pink in rich woodland. Takes 7–10 years to bloom from seed. Never pick — removing the leaves kills the plant. Ohio's state wildflower and one of the finest spring ephemerals of the eastern deciduous forest.

flowers.name: Wild Blue Phlox
flowers.wildlife: Attracts sphinx moths and swallowtail butterflies.
flowers.description: Fragrant pale lavender-blue flowers carpeting Ohio's rich woodland floors in spring. One of the finest native plants for shaded gardens — adaptable to both sun and shade, spreads to form beautiful drifts. The evening fragrance attracts sphinx moths.

flowers.name: Wild Ginger
flowers.description: Heart-shaped aromatic leaves forming dense ground cover in Ohio's rich woodland, hiding small brownish-red flowers at soil level. The roots have an authentic ginger scent and were used as a spice substitute. One of the finest native ground covers for deep shade.

flowers.name: Bloodroot
flowers.description: One of Ohio's first spring wildflowers — pure white blooms with golden stamens emerging before the trees leaf out. Brilliant orange-red sap in the root. Disappears completely by summer. Found in particularly fine stands in the Hocking Hills region.

flowers.name: Cardinal Flower
flowers.description: Brilliant scarlet flower spikes along Ohio's streams and wetland edges. The defining hummingbird plant of the Midwest — tubular flowers perfectly designed for Ruby-throated Hummingbird pollination. One of the most valuable native plants for attracting hummingbirds to Ohio gardens.

flowers.name: Prairie Trillium
flowers.description: A distinctive trillium of Ohio's prairie-forest transition zone — dark maroon-red petals with mottled leaves. Found in the western Ohio woodlands where prairie and forest once met. Named for the recurved (bent-back) sepals that distinguish it from other trilliums.

flowers.name: Yellow Coneflower
flowers.habitat: Prairies, dry open woodland — native prairie remnants
flowers.wildlife: Goldfinches eat seeds. Native bees and butterflies.
flowers.description: A prairie native found in Ohio's remnant tallgrass prairie habitats — drooping yellow ray petals around a distinctive elongated gray-brown center cone. Found in the scattered prairie openings and dry open woodlands of western Ohio. An important component of Ohio's rapidly disappearing native prairie ecosystem.

flowers.name: Virginia Bluebell
flowers.wildlife: Queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: Masses of sky-blue nodding tubular flowers in Ohio's floodplain forests — one of the most beautiful spring wildflowers. Pink buds open to blue flowers. A true spring ephemeral — completely dormant by early summer. Found in spectacular drifts along Ohio's major river floodplains.

flowers.name: Shooting Star
flowers.wildlife: Buzz-pollinated by bumblebees — unique feeding behavior.
flowers.description: One of Ohio's most distinctive wildflowers — swept-back pink petals giving the appearance of a shooting star in flight. Pollinated by bumblebees using 'buzz pollination' — the bee vibrates at a specific frequency to dislodge pollen. A declining prairie and open woodland species in Ohio.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Peony
flowers.description: Indiana's state flower is the peony — chosen in 1957. Not a native wildflower but enormously popular in Indiana gardens. The peony is among the most long-lived garden plants — some Indiana peonies have been blooming for over 50 years.

flowers.name: Dutchman's Breeches
flowers.description: White pantaloon-shaped flowers dangling from arching stems in Indiana's rich woodland ravines. A spring ephemeral pollinated exclusively by long-tongued queen bumblebees. Indiana's unglaciated south contains some of the finest spring ephemeral wildflower communities in the Midwest.

flowers.name: Wild Columbine
flowers.description: Red and yellow spurred flowers of Indiana's rocky woodland slopes and sandstone cliff faces. The first hummingbird flower of spring in Indiana — critical fuel for northward-migrating Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. Self-seeds in appropriate conditions.

flowers.name: Prairie Blazing Star
flowers.wildlife: Essential Monarch butterfly plant. Native bee specialist.
flowers.description: Tall magenta-purple flower spikes of Indiana's original tallgrass prairie — now reduced to less than 1% of its original extent. This blazing star blooms from the top downward, unusual among spike flowers. A critical Monarch butterfly fueling station and native bee specialist. Indiana's prairie preserves protect some of the last examples.

flowers.name: Blue Wild Indigo
flowers.habitat: Open woodland, prairie edges, dry slopes
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Wild Indigo Duskywing butterfly.
flowers.description: Deep blue-purple pea-like flowers on a bold 3–4 foot plant of Indiana's open woodland and prairie edges. Extremely long-lived — individual plants survive 50+ years. Nitrogen-fixing roots. Striking black seed pods in fall. The roots were used as a dye substitute for true indigo by early Indiana settlers.

flowers.name: Mayapple
flowers.wildlife: Yellow fruit eaten by box turtles and opossums.
flowers.description: Large umbrella-like leaves in dense colonies across Indiana's woodland floors, hiding a single waxy white flower. Only the forked two-leaved plants produce flowers and edible yellow fruit. Colonies may be centuries old — a single colony covering an acre may be one genetic individual. All parts except ripe fruit highly toxic.

flowers.name: Purple Coneflower
flowers.description: One of Indiana's most important native wildflowers — naturally found in the open woodland and prairie openings of the central and southern part of the state. Goldfinches depend on the seed heads through winter. Supports 50+ bee species. Also medicinally significant — the root of this species is the most commonly used echinacea in herbal medicine.

flowers.name: Wild Bergamot
flowers.description: Lavender-pink bee balm of Indiana's dry prairies and open woodland — one of the most important native plants for bee diversity. Aromatic minty-oregano fragrance. The leaves were used as a cooking and medicinal herb by indigenous peoples of the Great Plains. Drought-tolerant once established.

flowers.name: Swamp Rose Mallow
flowers.wildlife: Specialist native bees evolved for this genus.
flowers.description: Enormous native hibiscus with dinner-plate flowers along Indiana's wetland margins and pond edges. Among the largest flowers of any native plant in the Midwest. Specialist native bees in the genera Ptilothrix and Cemolobus evolved specifically to collect pollen from native Hibiscus — these bees cannot survive without it.

flowers.name: Spiderwort
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees. Unique pollen color.
flowers.description: Deep purple-blue three-petaled flowers with fuzzy yellow stamens found in Indiana's prairies and open areas. Named 'ohiensis' but actually native throughout the Midwest. The cells of the stamens are remarkably visible — used as a teaching tool for observing cell division. Sap turns pink-purple in response to environmental pollutants.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Violet
flowers.wildlife: Host for all Fritillary butterfly species.
flowers.description: Illinois's state flower — the native blue violet. The only larval host plant for all Fritillary butterfly species. Found throughout Illinois from prairies to woodland edges. Also edible — flowers and young leaves used in salads and as garnish.

flowers.name: Prairie Phlox
flowers.description: Fragrant pink prairie phlox of Illinois's original tallgrass prairie — one of the most beautiful prairie wildflowers. Found in the scattered prairie remnants that survive across Illinois, including the famous Midewin National Tallgrass Prairie. Hairy stems give it a distinctive texture. Threatened by prairie loss.

flowers.name: Prairie Smoke
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies, rocky slopes — Illinois's northern tier
flowers.wildlife: Early bee plant. Feathery seed heads.
flowers.description: One of the most distinctive prairie wildflowers — nodding pink flowers that look like smoking pipes, followed by the extraordinary feathery seed heads that give it the name 'prairie smoke.' A plant of dry, undisturbed prairie in northern Illinois. The feathery seedheads catch the light like pink smoke across the prairie.

flowers.name: Compass Plant
flowers.wildlife: Goldfinches eat seeds. Native bee specialist.
flowers.description: A towering prairie plant reaching 8–10 feet — its basal leaves orient north-south (hence 'compass plant') and were used by prairie travelers for navigation. One of the most ecologically significant prairie indicator species — its presence signals undisturbed prairie. Deep taproot reaches 15 feet. Once common in Illinois; now found only in protected prairie remnants.

flowers.name: Shooting Star
flowers.description: Illinois's most distinctive spring wildflower — swept-back pink petals forming the shooting star shape. Buzz-pollinated by bumblebees at a specific vibration frequency. Found in both prairie and woodland habitats across Illinois. A declining species as prairie and open woodland habitats disappear.

flowers.name: Wild Lupine
flowers.habitat: Sandy barrens, dry open areas — northern Illinois
flowers.wildlife: Sole host plant for Karner Blue butterfly.
flowers.description: Tall purple-blue flower spikes in Illinois's sandy barrens and dry open areas. The only host plant for the federally endangered Karner Blue butterfly — without wild lupine, this butterfly cannot survive. Illinois protects critical lupine populations in the sand country of the Illinois River valley.

flowers.name: Golden Alexanders
flowers.habitat: Moist prairies, open woodland, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Black Swallowtail butterfly. Early bee plant.
flowers.description: Bright yellow flat-topped flower clusters in spring — one of the earliest-blooming prairie wildflowers and the first yellow native of the season. Host plant for Black Swallowtail butterfly caterpillars. Found in moist prairies and open woodland throughout Illinois. One of the most garden-worthy native wildflowers.

flowers.name: Bur Oak
flowers.wildlife: Supports 534 moth/butterfly species — most of any Midwest oak.
flowers.description: Not a wildflower but the keystone plant of Illinois's prairie-savanna ecosystem. The massive bur oak — with its fire-resistant corky bark — was the dominant tree of the oak savanna that covered millions of Illinois acres. Supports 534 moth and butterfly species — more than any other Midwest plant. Old bur oaks are irreplaceable ecological treasures.

flowers.name: Prairie Dropseed
flowers.habitat: Dry to mesic prairies — prairie indicator grass
flowers.wildlife: Seeds eaten by sparrows. Habitat for insects.
flowers.description: An exceptional native grass of Illinois's high-quality prairies — dense mounds of fine-textured foliage with aromatic seed heads that smell of buttered popcorn or coriander. One of the most beautiful native grasses for garden use. A strong indicator of undisturbed, high-quality prairie — finding it signals a special remnant.

flowers.name: Pale Purple Coneflower
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies and rocky open areas — prairie specialist
flowers.description: The prairie-specialist coneflower of Illinois — pale lavender-pink drooping petals on a prominent dark center cone. More drought-tolerant and more narrowly prairie-adapted than E. purpurea. Found in the dry, rocky prairie remnants of western and central Illinois. The roots were the primary echinacea species used medicinally by Plains tribes.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Apple Blossom
flowers.habitat: State symbol — orchards and open areas
flowers.description: Michigan's state flower — the apple blossom, honoring Michigan's enormous importance as an apple-producing state. Michigan is among the top apple-producing states, and the pink and white blossoms of apple orchards are a quintessential Michigan spring sight.

flowers.name: Dwarf Lake Iris
flowers.habitat: Shorelines of the Great Lakes — extremely restricted range
flowers.description: Michigan's most famous native orchid — actually a tiny iris found only on the limestone shorelines of the Great Lakes, primarily in Michigan's Upper Peninsula. Federally threatened. Brilliant blue-violet flowers just 2–3 inches tall emerging from limestone rubble along Lake Superior and Lake Michigan shores. One of the rarest native plants in North America.

flowers.name: Pitcher's Thistle
flowers.habitat: Great Lakes sand dunes — federally threatened
flowers.wildlife: Important dune bee plant. Federally threatened.
flowers.description: A federally threatened native thistle found only on the sand dunes of the Great Lakes — primarily Michigan's Lake Michigan shoreline. Creamy-white flowers on a silvery-woolly plant adapted to shifting sand dunes. Takes 5–8 years to bloom, then dies after flowering. The Poweshiek skipperling butterfly depends on thistle species like this one.

flowers.name: Pink Lady's Slipper
flowers.description: Michigan's most celebrated native orchid — pink slipper-shaped flowers in acidic pine and bog woodland. Takes 10–17 years to bloom from seed. Requires specific mycorrhizal fungi — never transplant. Found throughout Michigan's northern counties in the undisturbed forest floor under pines and in sphagnum bogs.

flowers.name: Trillium (Nodding)
flowers.description: A distinctive trillium of Michigan's cool moist woodland — white flowers that nod downward on a bent stalk, hidden beneath the leaves. Found throughout Michigan's forested regions. The nodding position is unique among eastern trilliums and is an adaptation for pollination by ground-level insects.

flowers.name: Michigan Lily
flowers.habitat: Moist prairies, wetland edges — Michigan native
flowers.description: Michigan's native lily — brilliant orange-red reflexed petals with maroon spots on tall stems in moist prairies and wetland edges. Named for Michigan. Similar to Turk's Cap lily but more specifically native to the Great Lakes region. Now uncommon due to habitat loss and deer browsing.

flowers.name: Twinflower
flowers.description: A charming boreal forest plant of Michigan's Upper Peninsula — pairs of tiny nodding pink bells on thread-like stems, intensely fragrant. Named in honor of Carl Linnaeus, the father of botanical taxonomy, who reportedly loved this plant above all others. Found in the cool, mossy boreal forest floors of northern Michigan.

flowers.name: Fringed Gentian
flowers.description: One of Michigan's most beautiful and elusive wildflowers — intensely blue fringed petals that close in clouds and at night, opening only in full sun. Annual or biennial — appears unpredictably. Sensitive to habitat disturbance. A highlight of any Michigan fall wildflower walk in calcareous fens and stream banks.

flowers.name: Wild Lupine
flowers.habitat: Sandy barrens and dry open areas
flowers.wildlife: Sole host plant for Karner Blue butterfly.
flowers.description: Michigan hosts the largest remaining populations of the federally endangered Karner Blue butterfly — and wild lupine is the reason. This beautiful prairie plant of sandy barrens is the butterfly's only larval host plant. Michigan's oak-pine barrens contain critical lupine habitats. Without lupine, the Karner Blue cannot survive.

flowers.name: Thimbleweed
flowers.wildlife: Native bee plant. Persistent seed heads.
flowers.description: White five-petaled flowers followed by the distinctive thimble-shaped woolly seed heads that persist through winter. Found throughout Michigan's open woodlands and prairies. The persistent seed heads provide habitat for small insects through winter. One of the most recognizable native wildflowers for its distinctive fruiting structure.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Wood Violet
flowers.wildlife: Host for all Fritillary butterfly species.
flowers.description: Wisconsin's state flower — the wood violet, same species as Illinois and other states. A native blue violet essential as the sole larval host plant for all Fritillary butterfly species. Common throughout Wisconsin's woodland edges and open areas.

flowers.name: Prairie Smoke
flowers.wildlife: Early bee plant. Feathery seed heads.
flowers.description: One of Wisconsin's most distinctive prairie wildflowers — nodding pink flowers followed by feathery pinkish seed heads that catch the light across dry prairies and rocky slopes. One of the earliest prairie flowers to bloom. Found in Wisconsin's prairie remnants and rocky limestone outcrops.

flowers.name: Lupine (Wild)
flowers.habitat: Sandy barrens — Wisconsin's central sands region
flowers.wildlife: Sole host plant for Karner Blue butterfly. Critical for species survival.
flowers.description: Wisconsin's central sand barrens region hosts critical populations of wild lupine — and with them, the federally endangered Karner Blue butterfly. The Wisconsin DNR has active programs to protect and restore lupine habitat. The brilliant blue-purple flower spikes are spectacular in May across the sandy pine barrens.

flowers.name: Yellow Lady's Slipper
flowers.habitat: Rich moist woodland and bog edges
flowers.description: A beautiful native orchid of Wisconsin's rich moist woodland and bog edges — yellow inflated pouch trapping bees that must push past the stigma and anthers to escape. Takes 10+ years to bloom from seed. Never pick or transplant. Found throughout Wisconsin's forested counties in undisturbed conditions.

flowers.name: Pasque Flower
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies and rocky bluffs — Wisconsin's Driftless Area
flowers.wildlife: Very early bee plant. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: One of the first prairie flowers of the Wisconsin spring — silky-haired purple flowers emerging from dry prairies and rocky bluffs, often through snow. Found in Wisconsin's Driftless Area and dry sandy prairies. Feathery seed heads persist through summer. A special early spring wildflower of Wisconsin's most scenic landscapes.

flowers.name: Water Lily (Fragrant)
flowers.habitat: Ponds, lakes, slow rivers — throughout Wisconsin
flowers.wildlife: Aquatic habitat. Seeds eaten by waterfowl.
flowers.description: The fragrant white water lily of Wisconsin's lakes and ponds — intensely fragrant flowers opening in the morning and closing by noon. Found throughout Wisconsin's thousands of glacial lakes. Provides critical aquatic habitat structure. The rhizomes were an important food source for Wisconsin's indigenous peoples.

flowers.name: Blue Flag Iris
flowers.wildlife: Native bee specialist. Important wetland plant.
flowers.description: Striking blue-violet iris of Wisconsin's wetlands and lake margins — one of the finest native plants for bog gardens and pond edges. Tolerates standing water. The state wildflower of Quebec. Found throughout Wisconsin's abundant wetland habitats, often forming spectacular colonies.

flowers.name: Bottle Gentian
flowers.habitat: Moist prairies, wet meadows, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: Bumblebee specialist — only strong bees open flowers.
flowers.description: Deep blue closed flowers that bumblebees must force open — one of Wisconsin's most striking autumn wildflowers. Found in moist prairies and wet meadows across the state. A true autumn flower that continues blooming into October. The closed flower is a remarkable adaptation that excludes smaller, less effective pollinators.

flowers.name: Joe-Pye Weed
flowers.wildlife: Attracts 18+ butterfly species. Critical late-season plant.
flowers.description: Tall mauve-purple flower clusters reaching 5–7 feet in Wisconsin's moist prairies and wetland edges. A powerhouse late-summer pollinator plant supporting 18+ butterfly species and dozens of native bees. The spotted stems (maculatum = spotted) distinguish this Midwest species from the plain-stemmed southern species.

flowers.name: Trout Lily
flowers.description: Mottled brown-and-green leaves resembling brook trout emerge in spectacular colonies in Wisconsin's rich woodland. The nodding yellow lily flowers are among the earliest spring wildflowers. Only a fraction of plants in a colony bloom in any given year — the rest are non-flowering individuals connected by underground stolons.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Pink and White Lady's Slipper
flowers.description: Minnesota's state flower — the showy lady's slipper, the largest native orchid in North America. Pink-veined white pouch up to 2 inches across. Protected by law in Minnesota — illegal to pick or transplant from the wild. Found in specialized bog and fen habitats. Takes up to 16 years to bloom from seed.

flowers.name: Bunchberry
flowers.description: Miniature dogwood ground cover of Minnesota's boreal forest — white flower bracts and brilliant red berry clusters. Spreads by rhizome to carpet forest floors in acidic boreal conditions. The flowers have one of the fastest petal movements in the plant kingdom. Common in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness.

flowers.name: Prairie Coneflower
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies and roadsides — western Minnesota
flowers.description: The Mexican hat coneflower of Minnesota's western prairies — distinctive elongated brown-purple cone with drooping yellow ray petals. Found in the remnant dry prairies of western Minnesota transitioning into the Great Plains. Exceptionally drought-tolerant and long-blooming. One of the most recognizable prairie wildflowers.

flowers.name: Large-flowered Trillium
flowers.description: Minnesota's most spectacular native trillium — enormous pure white flowers aging to pink. Found in southeastern Minnesota's rich 'Big Woods' deciduous forest. Takes 7–10 years to bloom from seed. The Big Woods — Minnesota's original deciduous forest — survives only in scattered remnants; these trillium colonies represent an ancient landscape.

flowers.name: Blazing Star (Northern)
flowers.wildlife: Critical Monarch and native bee plant.
flowers.description: Tall magenta-purple flower spikes of Minnesota's dry prairies and rocky bluffs — a critical fueling station for Monarch butterflies beginning their migration to Mexico. Blooms in late summer and fall when Monarchs are moving through. Native to the tallgrass prairie that once covered much of southern Minnesota.

flowers.name: Blue Giant Hyssop
flowers.description: Minnesota's native anise hyssop — tall spikes of blue-purple flowers with an intensely sweet anise/licorice fragrance. One of the most important native bee plants in the Midwest. The fragrant leaves were used as a tea and flavoring by the Ojibwe people. Readily self-seeds in appropriate conditions.

flowers.name: Tall Meadow Rue
flowers.description: A stately native plant of Minnesota's moist prairies and stream banks reaching 5–8 feet — airy clouds of tiny white flowers. Wind-pollinated — the flowers lack petals but have attractive stamens. Found throughout Minnesota's wetland margins and moist open areas. One of the tallest native wildflowers.

flowers.name: Wild Bergamot
flowers.description: Lavender-pink bee balm of Minnesota's dry prairies — one of the most important native plants for bee diversity. The aromatic leaves with oregano-like scent were used as a seasoning by indigenous peoples of the northern plains. Extremely drought-tolerant and adaptable. A prairie garden essential.

flowers.name: Pale Jewel Weed
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbirds and hawk moths. Explosive seed dispersal.
flowers.description: Yellow spotted touch-me-not of Minnesota's moist, shaded stream banks and woodland edges. The ripe seed pods explode when touched, flinging seeds several feet — hence 'touch-me-not.' The juice from crushed stems is a traditional remedy for poison ivy and stinging nettles — and often grows alongside these plants.

flowers.name: Wild Ginger
flowers.description: Heart-shaped aromatic leaves forming dense ground cover in Minnesota's rich woodland, hiding small brownish-red flowers at soil level. The authentic ginger-scented roots were used as a flavoring by the Ojibwe and other Great Lakes nations. One of the finest native ground covers for shaded Minnesota gardens.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Wild Prairie Rose
flowers.wildlife: Native bees. Rose hips eaten by birds.
flowers.description: Iowa's state flower — the wild prairie rose, a native rose of Iowa's original tallgrass prairie. Simple pink five-petaled flowers with golden stamens. Produces rose hips eaten by birds through winter. Iowa's original tallgrass prairie has been almost entirely converted to agriculture — this prairie rose is a living remnant of the pre-settlement landscape.

flowers.name: Prairie Blazing Star
flowers.description: Tall magenta-purple flower spikes of Iowa's original moist tallgrass prairie — now reduced to tiny remnants. This is one of the most important plants for Monarch butterflies passing through Iowa on their fall migration. Iowa's prairie remnants, though small, provide critical fueling stations for Monarchs making the long journey to Mexico.

flowers.name: Prairie Coneflower
flowers.description: The classic gray-headed coneflower of Iowa's dry prairies — drooping yellow ray petals and a distinctive elongated gray cone. The most visible remnant of Iowa's original prairie along roadsides and in preserved natural areas. Iowa once had 30 million acres of tallgrass prairie — now less than 0.1% survives.

flowers.name: Wild Columbine
flowers.habitat: Rocky woodland and bluffs along Iowa's rivers
flowers.description: Red and yellow spurred flowers of Iowa's rocky woodland and river bluffs — particularly spectacular along the bluffs of the Mississippi and Missouri rivers. One of the most elegant native wildflowers. The first hummingbird flower of Iowa spring. Self-seeds freely in rocky, thin-soiled conditions.

flowers.name: Swamp Milkweed
flowers.description: Pink milkweed of Iowa's wetland margins — an essential Monarch butterfly host plant. Iowa is a critical corridor for Monarch migration — millions of butterflies pass through each fall. Milkweed is their only larval host plant. Iowa has lost over 98% of its milkweed due to herbicide-resistant crop systems — restoration is urgently needed.

flowers.name: Wild Ginger
flowers.description: Heart-shaped aromatic leaves forming dense ground cover along Iowa's rich river bluff woodland. The ginger-scented roots were used as a seasoning and medicine by the Sauk, Meskwaki, and other Iowa nations. One of the finest native ground covers for shaded conditions in Iowa's woodland gardens.

flowers.name: Blue Wild Indigo
flowers.wildlife: Host for Wild Indigo Duskywing butterfly.
flowers.description: Deep blue-purple pea-like flowers on a bold 3–4 foot plant found in Iowa's open woodland and remnant prairie edges. Extremely long-lived — 50+ years. The deep blue color is striking in the late spring landscape. Black seed pods rattle through winter. Nitrogen-fixing roots improve the soil.

flowers.name: Shooting Star
flowers.description: Iowa's most distinctive spring wildflower — swept-back pink petals forming the shooting star silhouette. Found in prairie remnants and open woodland throughout Iowa. Buzz-pollinated by bumblebees using sonic vibration. A declining species as prairie habitats are lost to agriculture.

flowers.name: Compass Plant
flowers.description: The great compass plant of Iowa's remaining prairie — leaves orient north-south and were used for navigation by pre-settlement travelers. Can reach 10 feet tall. Deep taproot extends 15+ feet. Once defining the Iowa landscape, now found only in protected prairie remnants and roadsides. An irreplaceable remnant of the original landscape.

flowers.name: Butterfly Weed
flowers.habitat: Dry, sandy, well-drained slopes and prairies
flowers.wildlife: Essential Monarch host. Most insect-rich native plant.
flowers.description: Brilliant orange milkweed of Iowa's dry sandy prairies — one of the most insect-attractive native plants available. Essential Monarch butterfly host plant. Unlike common milkweed, prefers dry sandy soil. The deep taproot makes it drought-resistant and impossible to transplant successfully — start from seed or purchase container-grown plants.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: White Hawthorn Blossom
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by 40+ bird species. Caterpillar host plant.
flowers.description: Missouri's state flower — the white hawthorn blossom. Missouri has more native hawthorn species than any other state. The fragrant white flower clusters in spring are followed by small red or orange berries (haws) eaten by 40+ bird species. Hawthorns support an extraordinary range of native wildlife.

flowers.name: Wild Blue Phlox
flowers.description: Fragrant lavender-blue flowers carpeting Missouri's rich Ozark woodland floors in spring. Missouri's Ozarks contain some of the finest spring wildflower communities in the Midwest — rich with trilliums, phlox, columbine, and May apple. The evening fragrance of wild blue phlox fills the woodland air.

flowers.name: Pawpaw
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Zebra Swallowtail butterfly. Fruit eaten by wildlife.
flowers.description: Missouri's most distinctive native fruit tree — maroon flowers in early spring, followed by the largest edible fruit native to North America. The custard-like yellow flesh tastes of banana, vanilla, and mango. The Zebra Swallowtail butterfly depends exclusively on pawpaw as its larval host. Mark Twain wrote fondly of pawpaws from his Missouri childhood.

flowers.name: Fire Pink
flowers.habitat: Rocky woodland, dry slopes, cliff edges — Ozarks
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbird specialist. Bright red signals hummingbird vision.
flowers.description: Brilliant scarlet star-shaped flowers of Missouri's rocky Ozark woodland and cliff faces. The deep red color and tubular shape specifically attract Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. One of Missouri's most striking native wildflowers. The Ozark region of Missouri contains exceptional diversity of native wildflowers.

flowers.name: Coneflower (Purple)
flowers.description: Missouri is one of the centers of diversity for purple coneflower — naturally found in the open woodland and prairie openings throughout the state. Missouri's native coneflower populations predate the plant's rise to garden fame. Critical for pollinator diversity and Monarch migration fueling.

flowers.name: Wild Blue Indigo
flowers.habitat: Open woodland, rocky glades — Ozark specialty
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for multiple butterfly species.
flowers.description: Deep blue-purple pea flowers on a bold prairie plant — found in Missouri's open woodland, rocky glades, and prairie edges. The Ozark glades (dry, rocky open areas) are one of Missouri's most biodiverse ecosystems and a stronghold for blue wild indigo. Lives 50+ years.

flowers.name: Shooting Star
flowers.description: Missouri's most distinctive spring wildflower — swept-back pink petals in the shooting star formation. Found in Missouri's prairies, rocky glades, and open woodland. Missouri has exceptional populations in the Ozark region. Buzz-pollinated by bumblebees at a specific resonant frequency.

flowers.name: Indian Pink
flowers.description: One of Missouri's most spectacular native wildflowers — brilliant red tubular flowers with yellow interiors on upright stems in rich Ozark woodland. Designed exclusively for hummingbird pollination. The Ozarks are a stronghold for Indian pink — Missouri populations represent some of the most northern occurrences of this southeastern species.

flowers.name: Goldenrod (Stiff)
flowers.wildlife: Supports 115+ bee species. Critical fall pollinator plant.
flowers.description: A golden-topped prairie goldenrod of Missouri's dry prairies and rocky glades — flat-topped golden flower clusters on stiff, rigid stems. One of the most ecologically important native plants for late-season pollinators preparing for winter. Despite being mistakenly blamed for hay fever (it's ragweed that causes allergies), goldenrod is entirely insect-pollinated.

flowers.name: Wild Ginger
flowers.description: Heart-shaped aromatic leaves forming dense ground cover in Missouri's rich Ozark woodland. The authentic ginger-scented roots were used as a spice substitute. The Osage, Missouri, and other Missouri nations used wild ginger extensively as food and medicine. One of the finest native ground covers for shaded Missouri woodland gardens.
